claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy contains dissimilar phases with different electrochemical potentials.
A protective oxide film is pre-formed on at least one phase.
Micro-galvanic coupling between dissimilar eutectic phases drives synergistic wear-corrosion degradation.
Mechanical wear at elevated temperature continuously removes or thins protective oxide on the more corrosion-resistant phase.
The less noble phase undergoes accelerated selective or localized corrosion because of micro-galvanic coupling with the other phase.
Micro-galvanic corrosion is concentrated along phase boundaries and interfacial regions.
Corrosion weakens phase boundaries and interfacial regions.
Corrosion-induced interfacial weakening increases mechanical material removal.
Mutual enhancement of corrosion and wear creates a positive feedback loop that accelerates overall degradation.
The proposed mechanism is relevant at approximately 450–650 °C in an acidic or molten-salt environment under concurrent mechanical contact.
Combined wear-corrosion produces a higher total degradation rate than isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Combined exposure increases the wear rate relative to isolated wear.
Combined exposure increases pitting or selective dissolution relative to static corrosion.
Combined degradation exceeds the sum of the degradation measured in isolated wear and isolated corrosion tests.
The oxide film remains relatively undisturbed during the isolated static-corrosion baseline.
Electrochemical contrast between constituent phases is a boundary condition for the proposed micro-galvanic mechanism.
Mechanical compromise of the oxide film is a boundary condition for the proposed positive feedback mechanism.
Scanning Kelvin probe measurements can detect the Volta-potential difference associated with micro-galvanic coupling between phases.
A robust coating or engineered oxide will minimize galvanic effects under combined wear-corrosion exposure.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts that suppressing galvanic coupling with a coating should eliminate or reduce superadditive degradation, but the falsification rule states that failure of the coated samples to exceed additive wear-plus-corrosion effects would falsify the mechanism. That outcome would instead be consistent with successful suppression of the proposed coupling.
